question: An operator wants direct evidence of ammonia removal across one aeration basin during a single shift. Which pair of samples gives that evidence?
correctAnswer: Ammonia at the basin inlet and ammonia at the basin outlet that day
explanation: Ammonia measured at the inlet and outlet of the same basin over the same period shows what that basin removed. Samples from other locations or other days mix in effects from other process stages.
options: Ammonia at the basin inlet and ammonia at the basin outlet that day
Ammonia in the raw influent and nitrate in the final effluent that week
Ammonia in the return sludge and alkalinity at the basin outlet that day
Ammonia at the basin outlet and phosphorus at the basin inlet that day
sourceTitle: US EPA: Municipal Wastewater — supporting treatment resources
sourceReference: Supporting resource category: Nutrient Testing Awareness. See SOURCES.md: these are not claim-level verification citations.
optionA: Ammonia at the basin inlet and ammonia at the basin outlet that day
optionB: Ammonia in the raw influent and nitrate in the final effluent that week
optionC: Ammonia in the return sludge and alkalinity at the basin outlet that day
optionD: Ammonia at the basin outlet and phosphorus at the basin inlet that day

question: A laboratory reports orthophosphate separately from total phosphorus for a wastewater sample. What does the orthophosphate result represent?
correctAnswer: The dissolved reactive phosphorus in a filtered sample, ready for uptake
explanation: Orthophosphate is the dissolved reactive fraction measured on a filtered sample. Total phosphorus needs digestion and includes particulate and condensed forms, so it is normally higher.
options: The phosphorus bound inside suspended solids in the unfiltered sample only
The dissolved reactive phosphorus in a filtered sample, ready for uptake
The phosphorus released only after a strong acid digestion of the sample
The phosphorus stored inside bacterial cells and measured after settling
sourceTitle: US EPA: Municipal Wastewater — supporting treatment resources
sourceReference: Supporting resource category: Phosphorus Awareness. See SOURCES.md: these are not claim-level verification citations.
optionA: The phosphorus bound inside suspended solids in the unfiltered sample only
optionB: The dissolved reactive phosphorus in a filtered sample, ready for uptake
optionC: The phosphorus released only after a strong acid digestion of the sample
optionD: The phosphorus stored inside bacterial cells and measured after settling

question: An online dissolved oxygen probe reads steadily while portable meter checks at the same spot climb week by week. Which record best confirms probe drift?
correctAnswer: Paired online and portable readings recorded on several days
explanation: Paired readings taken at the same place and time on several days show a growing gap that points to drift. A single unmatched reading cannot separate probe error from a real process change.
options: A single grab result taken during a rainstorm last month
The blower run hours logged on the previous weekend shift
Paired online and portable readings recorded on several days
The basin temperature noted once at the start of the season
sourceTitle: US EPA - Resources for Wastewater Operators

optionA: A single grab result taken during a rainstorm last month
optionB: The blower run hours logged on the previous weekend shift
optionC: Paired online and portable readings recorded on several days
optionD: The basin temperature noted once at the start of the season

question: In a centrifugal wastewater pump, which component converts the high velocity leaving the impeller into pressure?
correctAnswer: The volute casing that surrounds the impeller discharge area
explanation: The expanding volute casing slows the liquid leaving the impeller and converts velocity into pressure. Wear rings, couplings and check valves each serve different mechanical duties.
options: The shaft coupling that joins the motor shaft to the pump
The wear ring that limits leakage back to the suction side
The volute casing that surrounds the impeller discharge area
The check valve that prevents reverse flow in the discharge

optionD: The check valve that prevents reverse flow in the discharge

question: An operator raises the waste activated sludge rate while influent load and basin volume stay the same. What happens to sludge age?
correctAnswer: It falls because solids now leave the system at a faster rate
explanation: Sludge age is the time solids spend in the system, so removing solids faster shortens that time. Higher wasting lowers inventory and gives a younger sludge unless load changes offset it.
options: It stays unchanged because basin volume has not changed at all
It rises because solids now remain in the system for much longer
It doubles because wasted solids return through the return sludge
It falls because solids now leave the system at a faster rate
sourceTitle: WPI: 2025 Need-to-Know criteria

optionD: It falls because solids now leave the system at a faster rate

question: A microscopic look at activated sludge shows many filamentous organisms bridging between flocs, and the sludge settles poorly. What condition does this picture support?
correctAnswer: Filamentous bulking that keeps flocs apart and slows settling in the clarifier
explanation: Filaments bridging between flocs hold the blanket open so it cannot compact, which is filamentous bulking. The settleometer and microscope together confirm the pattern before changes are made.
options: Filamentous bulking that keeps flocs apart and slows settling in the clarifier
Healthy pin floc that settles quickly and leaves a very clear supernatant layer
Complete nitrification that removes ammonia and leaves the blanket compact and dense
Dispersed growth caused by a sudden toxic discharge that killed all the filaments

optionB: Healthy pin floc that settles quickly and leaves a very clear supernatant layer
optionC: Complete nitrification that removes ammonia and leaves the blanket compact and dense
optionD: Dispersed growth caused by a sudden toxic discharge that killed all the filaments

question: In a final clarifier, clumps of sludge rise to the surface carrying small gas bubbles on a warm afternoon. Which process in the blanket most likely produced the gas?
correctAnswer: Denitrification in the deep blanket converting nitrate into nitrogen gas
explanation: With oxygen depleted in a deep blanket, bacteria use nitrate and release nitrogen gas, which lifts sludge clumps. Warm weather speeds the reaction, so the blanket depth and return rate need attention.
options: Nitrification in the aeration basin converting ammonia into nitrate earlier
Denitrification in the deep blanket converting nitrate into nitrogen gas
Photosynthesis in the clarifier surface algae releasing oxygen into the water
Fermentation in the primary clarifier producing methane under the scum layer

optionD: Fermentation in the primary clarifier producing methane under the scum layer

question: A wet well is classed as a confined space and a worker must enter it for a pump repair. Which step comes before anyone enters?
correctAnswer: Testing the atmosphere from outside the space with a calibrated gas meter
explanation: Atmospheric testing is done from outside with a calibrated meter before entry, and ventilation and permits support that result. Smell is unreliable, especially for hydrogen sulfide, which dulls the sense of smell.
options: Sending the first worker in quickly to check whether the air smells acceptable
Lowering the rescue tripod into the space so it is ready for the entry team
Testing the atmosphere from outside the space with a calibrated gas meter
Starting the ventilation fan only after the worker reaches the pump level

question: Final effluent ammonia is very low, but effluent nitrate has climbed well above its usual range. What does this pairing tell the operator?
correctAnswer: Nitrification is working, but denitrification is limited in the anoxic zone
explanation: Low ammonia with high nitrate means ammonia was oxidized but the nitrate was not then reduced. The operator should check anoxic zone carbon, mixing and internal recycle rather than aeration capacity.
options: Nitrification is working, but denitrification is limited in the anoxic zone
Nitrification has stopped, and ammonia is passing through the plant untreated
Denitrification is complete, and most nitrogen has already left as nitrogen gas
The laboratory has swapped the ammonia and nitrate results on the report sheet

question: A plant adds alum for phosphorus removal. Why does the feed point location, upstream of the final clarifier rather than after it, matter?
correctAnswer: Precipitate formed upstream is captured with the clarifier solids and removed
explanation: Alum reacts with phosphorus to form a precipitate that must be settled out with the solids. Feeding after the clarifier leaves that precipitate with no settling step, so it can leave with the effluent.
options: Alum fed after the clarifier removes phosphorus without forming any new solids
Precipitate formed upstream dissolves again before it reaches the clarifier inlet
Alum fed upstream changes the influent flow measurement at the headworks meter
Precipitate formed upstream is captured with the clarifier solids and removed
sourceTitle: US EPA: Municipal Wastewater — supporting treatment resources

question: At 2 a.m. the trend screen shows influent flow doubled, yet wet well level, pump status and rainfall are all unchanged. What should the operator do first?

options: Double the chemical feed rates to match the flow shown on the trend screen
Record the doubled flow in the log and take no further action until next week
Shut down one aeration basin until the morning shift reviews the flow records
Field check the flow meter and look for fouling or a sensor fault at the site

question: A lift station pump rattles like gravel and its discharge pressure swings. The wet well level is near the pump intake. Which check addresses the likely cause?
correctAnswer: Check for low suction level and a partly blocked suction line causing cavitation
explanation: Noise like gravel with swinging pressure at low suction level points to cavitation, where vapour bubbles form and collapse. Raising the level and clearing the suction path remove the conditions that cause it.
options: Check for low suction level and a partly blocked suction line causing cavitation
Check the discharge check valve seat for wear that lets flow run back at shutdown
Check the motor starter heater sizing against the nameplate full load current rating
Check the station ventilation rate against the design value for the below grade room

question: Cold weather arrives and effluent ammonia starts rising because nitrifiers grow slowly at low temperature. Which wasting decision best protects nitrification?
correctAnswer: Reduce wasting to hold an older sludge age and keep more nitrifiers in the basin
explanation: Nitrifiers grow slowly, so a longer sludge age keeps enough of them in the system during cold weather. Reducing wasting raises sludge age, though clarifier loading still has to be watched.
options: Waste heavily for one week so only the youngest, fastest growing solids remain
Stop wasting entirely for the season and let mixed liquor climb without any limit
Reduce wasting to hold an older sludge age and keep more nitrifiers in the basin
Waste from the clarifier surface so the oldest solids stay settled in the blanket

correctAnswer: Raise basin dissolved oxygen and hold it steady through the high load period

Raise basin dissolved oxygen and hold it steady through the high load period

Add alum at the headworks to coat the filaments and weigh the flocs down fast

Raise the return sludge rate to pull the blanket down and shorten blanket time
Stop wasting for a week so the blanket has more time to compact in the clarifier

question: A report lists total Kjeldahl nitrogen well above the ammonia result for the same sample. What accounts for the difference between the two values?
correctAnswer: The Kjeldahl result includes organic nitrogen in addition to the ammonia nitrogen
explanation: Total Kjeldahl nitrogen is ammonia nitrogen plus organic nitrogen, so it exceeds the ammonia result whenever organic nitrogen is present. Nitrate and nitrite are not included in the Kjeldahl fraction.
options: The ammonia result includes organic nitrogen that the Kjeldahl digestion leaves out
The Kjeldahl result measures nitrate that the ammonia test converts during storage
The Kjeldahl result includes organic nitrogen in addition to the ammonia nitrogen
The difference is a reporting error, because the two tests measure the same fraction

Bacteria absorb extra phosphorus into their cells faster than they can use it there
Alum in the zone binds phosphorus into a precipitate that settles in the clarifier
Phosphorus is converted into a gas that leaves the basin through the surface foam

question: Two identical pumps are piped in parallel at a lift station and both are started together. What should the operator expect compared with one pump running?
correctAnswer: More flow delivered against roughly the same head as one pump on its own
explanation: Pumps in parallel add their flows at a similar head, while pumps in series add head at a similar flow. The actual gain is less than double because friction losses rise as flow increases.
options: Roughly double the head at exactly the same flow as a single pump station
More flow delivered against roughly the same head as one pump on its own
Exactly double the flow at double the head that one pump produces by itself
The same flow as one pump, with the second pump adding only standby capacity

question: An operator keeps wasting the same volume each day, but return sludge solids concentration drops, so the mass wasted each day falls. What happens to sludge age?
correctAnswer: It rises, because less solid mass is leaving the system each day now

It falls, because the wasted volume controls sludge age on its own
It stays the same, because sludge age ignores wasted mass entirely
It cannot change until the basin volume or influent flow is altered

question: A pump that used to run mid curve now runs far out on its curve after a discharge valve was left fully open and a parallel main came back in service. What risk does that operating point carry?
correctAnswer: Higher flow at lower head, with motor overload and cavitation becoming more likely
explanation: Running far out on the curve means high flow against low system head, which can overload the motor and starve the suction side into cavitation. Restoring the normal system resistance moves the duty point back.
options: Higher flow at lower head, with motor overload and cavitation becoming more likely
Lower flow at higher head, with the motor running cooler than its design point allows
No added risk, because a centrifugal pump is protected at every point on its curve

question: In winter a plant needs a long sludge age for nitrification, but the final clarifier is already near its solids loading limit. Which plan respects both limits?
correctAnswer: Hold the longest practical sludge age and watch clarifier loading and blanket closely
explanation: The operator balances the two constraints, keeping sludge age as long as the clarifier can carry while tracking blanket depth and solids loading daily. Ignoring either limit trades one failure for another.
options: Stop return sludge pumping so basin solids stay out of the clarifier during winter

question: Rising sludge is worst on warm afternoons, effluent nitrate is high, and extra return pumping earlier in the day prevents it. Why does the timing of return pumping matter so much here?
correctAnswer: Warm sludge denitrifies faster, so solids must spend less time sitting in the blanket
explanation: Higher temperature speeds denitrification in the blanket, so on warm days the same blanket depth produces gas sooner. Pulling solids back earlier shortens blanket time before gas can lift them.

Nitrate disappears in warm weather, so the blanket can safely be left deep all day long
